days.title: بلند شو!

steps.title: The Pattern: Commands
steps.content:
Mass says بلند شو (get up!), بیا (come!), برو (go!). These are informal imperatives — the way you tell someone to do something at home.

For most verbs, take the present stem and add بـ (be-) at the front:
steps.note: بیا (come) and برو (go) are irregular — they don't follow the بـ pattern. You just memorize them.

steps.title: Verb Forms: Commands
steps.explanation:
Today's verbs are all commands (imperatives). In spoken Farsi, you make a command by using the present stem. For compound verbs like بلند شدن, only the helper verb شدن conjugates.

Here are the three forms you need:
steps.note: بیا and برو are irregular — they don't follow the بـ + stem pattern. You just memorize them. For compound verbs (بلند شدن, بیدار شدن), only the شدن part conjugates.

steps.title: The Alphabet: ا ب پ
steps.instruction: Three letters you'll see in today's words. Each letter has up to four forms depending on where it appears in a word.

letters.name: alef
letters.tip: Alef never connects to the letter after it. When it carries an آ sound (with the hat), it's always at the start.

letters.name: be
letters.tip: The dot goes below. Compare with پ (three dots below) and ت (two dots above).

letters.name: pe
letters.tip: Same shape as ب but with three dots below. This letter doesn't exist in Arabic — it's uniquely Persian.

practice.prompt: Find the ا in this word: بیا
Write the word آب (water) — it uses two of today's letters.

steps.title: The Pattern: More Commands + "Don't"
steps.content:
You already know بیا and برو. Now add three more:

  • بشین beshin — sit down!
  • صبر کن sabr kon — wait!
  • ببین bebin — look!

To say don't, swap بـ for نـ (na-):
steps.note: The negative pattern: بشین (sit!) → نشین (don't sit!). The بـ becomes نـ.

steps.title: Verb Forms: At the Table
steps.explanation: Three more commands for breakfast. Notice the pattern: بـ + present stem for regular verbs. To say "don't," swap بـ for نـ.
steps.note: صبر کردن is a compound verb like بلند شدن — only the کردن part conjugates. The negative goes on the helper: صبر نکن.

steps.title: The Alphabet: ت ن م
steps.instruction: Three more letters from this week's vocabulary. Pay attention to the dots — they're the only difference between some of these shapes.

letters.name: te
letters.tip: Same body as ب and پ, but two dots above. At the end of a word it often looks like ـه.

letters.name: noon
letters.tip: One dot above, with a deeper bowl shape than ب. In initial form (نـ) it can look like بـ — watch for the dot position.

letters.name: mim
letters.tip: A round loop. In the middle of a word (ـمـ) it's a small bump on the baseline.

steps.title: New Words
steps.instruction: Today's words are about feelings and useful modifiers.

steps.title: The Pattern: Negatives + Modifiers
steps.content:
You've learned commands. Now learn to soften and negate them:

  • عجله نکن ajaleh nakon — Don't hurry (نکن = don't do)
  • دوباره بگو dobah-reh begoo — Say it again
  • یه کم صبر کن yeh kam sabr kon — Wait a little

یه کم (a little) and دوباره (again) are modifiers you can add to almost any sentence to make it more natural.
steps.note: حوصله ندارم (howseleh nadahram) means "I have no patience" or "I'm bored" — you'll use this one a lot!

steps.title: Verb Forms: How You Feel
steps.explanation: To say how you feel, attach the short pronoun suffix to the adjective. This is like saying "tired-am" instead of "I am tired." Here's the full pattern with خسته (tired):
steps.note: This works with any adjective: گشنمه (I'm hungry), تشنته (you're thirsty), خوشحالم (I'm happy), ناراحته (he/she is upset). In casual speech, من گشنمه is more natural than من گشنه‌ام.

options: I'm bored / I have no patience

steps.title: Read
steps.instruction: Read this passage. It uses only words you know. Try reading it aloud before checking the translation.

text.persian: صبح بخیر! بلند شو. صبحونه حاضره. بیا بشین. چای می‌خوای؟ آره ممنون. من گشنمه. صبر کن الان میارم. ببین چی درست کردم. خوشحالم ممنون!
text.pronunciation: sobh bekheyr! boland sho. sobhooneh hahzereh. bee-ah beshin. chahy mee-khahy? ah-reh mamnoon. man goshnameh. sabr kon alahn mee-ahram. bebin chee dorost kardam. khosh-hahlam mamnoon!
text.english: Good morning! Get up. Breakfast is ready. Come sit down. Do you want tea? Yes, thanks. I'm hungry. Wait, I'll bring it now. Look what I made. I'm happy, thanks!

model.persian: من یه کم خسته‌ام ولی خوشحالم. حوصله ندارم. دوباره چای می‌خوام.
model.pronunciation: man yeh kam khasteh-am valee khosh-hahlam. howseleh nadahram. dobah-reh chahy mee-khahm.
model.english: I'm a little tired but I'm happy. I'm bored. I want tea again.

steps.title: The Alphabet: خ چ ش
steps.instruction: Today's letters include some sounds that don't exist in English. Listen to the words to hear the difference.

letters.name: khe
letters.sound: kh (back-of-throat h, like clearing your throat gently)
letters.tip: Same shape as ح and ج but with a dot above. kh is NOT like English k — it's the sound you make when you say 'Bach' in German.

letters.name: che
letters.tip: Same shape as ج and خ but with three dots below. Like پ, this letter is uniquely Persian — Arabic doesn't have it.

letters.name: shin
letters.tip: Three teeth with three dots above. Compare with س (same shape, no dots).

practice.prompt: How is چ different from ج?

steps.title: Culture: Taarof at Breakfast
steps.content:
Taarof (تعارف) is the art of politeness in Persian culture. You'll hear it everywhere — at the table, at the door, even at the store. It's not just manners; it's a rhythm that every Iranian learns from childhood.

At breakfast, if Mass offers you tea, the taarof way is to first decline:

نه ممنون، زحمت نکش.
nah mamnoon, zahmat nakesh.
No thanks, don't trouble yourself.

Mass will insist — maybe two or three times. This is normal. When you finally accept, you show gratitude:

دستت درد نکنه.
dastet dard nakoneh.
Literally: "May your hand not hurt." (Thank you for the effort.)

You'll hear خواهش می‌کنم (khahesh mee-konam) constantly — it means "you're welcome" but literally "I beg of you." That captures the taarof spirit: everything is offered as if the other person is doing you a favor by accepting.

Tip: You don't need to do full taarof with Mass at home — she'll laugh if you refuse tea three times! But notice when she does it with guests or on the phone. It's one of the most beautiful parts of Persian culture.

steps.title: Teach the Girls
steps.instruction: Teaching someone else is the best way to learn. Here are five words and activities to try with your daughters this week.

activities.game: Play "Simon Says" in Farsi. Start with بیا (come!) and برو (go!). Use gestures so they connect the word to the action. Keep switching between the two until they react without thinking.
Every morning this week, say صبح بخیر to each girl when they wake up. By the weekend, see who says it first. Make it a race.
Replace "thank you" with ممنون for the whole week. Every time they say thanks in English, say "In Farsi?" and wait for ممنون.
At meals, ask "آب می‌خوای؟" (Do you want water?). They answer آره (yes) or نه (no). Simple call-and-response.
Play musical chairs in Farsi. When the music stops, yell بشین! They'll remember it after one round.
